long: Bitcoin is pseudonymous, not anonymous. Every transaction since the genesis block (Jan 3, 2009) is recorded on a public ledger that anyone can download and keep forever. Only the link between an address and a person is hidden, and that link can be found. Police have traced hackers, ransomware gangs and darknet admins through it for over a decade. The series explains how tracing works and what privacy tools really change.
tech: Crypto #Anonymity Myths #1: Bitcoin is pseudonymous, not anonymous. Every transaction since the genesis block (Jan 3, 2009) sits on a public ledger anyone can download. Privacy rests on one thing: nobody linking an address to you.
simple: Crypto #Anonymity Myths #1: Is Bitcoin anonymous? No. It is pseudonymous: every payment ever made is public, forever. Only the name behind each address is hidden, and that name can be found. This series shows how, and what real privacy takes.
variant: Crypto #Anonymity Myths #1: The biggest myth in crypto: "Bitcoin is anonymous." Police have traced hackers, ransomware gangs and darknet admins through it for over a decade. Let's look at how they do it, and what privacy tools really change.

card.title: Bitcoin is pseudonymous, not anonymous
card.sub: Every transaction since the genesis block is public. Only the link to a person is hidden.

long: Pseudonymity means one stable identifier with many actions attached to it, like a pen name. As long as nobody ties the address to a person, it looks private. But once a single address is linked to a real identity, for example through a KYC exchange withdrawal, a public donation page or a shop order, its entire past history and all its counterparties are exposed too, including old payments.
tech: Crypto #Anonymity Myths #2: Pseudonymity = one stable identifier with many actions attached. Once one address is tied to a real identity (KYC withdrawal, donation page, shop order), its whole history and counterparties are exposed.
simple: Crypto #Anonymity Myths #2: Think of a Bitcoin address as a pen name. Nobody knows who wrote the books, until one book is traced to you. Then every book under that pen name is yours too, including the old ones.

card.title: One address linked, whole history exposed
card.sub: A single KYC withdrawal or shop order can reveal all past payments and counterparties.

long: Satoshi flagged the limits in the Bitcoin whitepaper itself. Section 10, "Privacy", advises using a new key pair for each transaction to keep them from being linked to a common owner, but admits that "some linking is still unavoidable with multi-input transactions, which necessarily reveal that their inputs were owned by the same owner." The design never claimed full anonymity.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #3: Bitcoin whitepaper, section 10 "Privacy": use a new key pair for each transaction, but "some linking is still unavoidable with multi-input transactions, which necessarily reveal that their inputs were owned by the same owner."

The fresh key pair keeps payments from being tied to a common owner. Multi-input transactions break that, because they show one owner behind several inputs. The design never claimed full anonymity.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #3: Satoshi warned about this in the Bitcoin whitepaper itself. Section 10 says: use a new address for every payment, and know that some linking is still unavoidable.

Why? When one payment spends coins from several of your addresses, it shows they all belong to the same owner. So Bitcoin was never designed to be fully anonymous, and its creator said so from day one.

card.title: Satoshi warned about linking from day one
card.sub: The whitepaper admits multi-input transactions reveal a common owner.

long: Whitepaper section 10 contrasts Bitcoin with banks. The traditional model gets privacy by limiting access to records to the parties and a trusted third party. Bitcoin must announce every transaction publicly, so privacy can only come from keeping public keys anonymous, like a stock exchange tape that shows the time and size of trades but not who traded. Once a key is tied to a person, that privacy is gone.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #4: Whitepaper section 10: banks get privacy by limiting access to records to the parties and a trusted third party. Bitcoin announces every transaction, so privacy comes only from keeping public keys anonymous.

Satoshi's analogy: a stock exchange tape shows the time and size of each trade, but not who traded. Bitcoin works the same way. Once a key is tied to a person, that privacy is gone.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #4: The whitepaper compares Bitcoin to banks. A bank keeps your privacy by hiding its records. Bitcoin can't, since every record is public. Its only privacy is keeping addresses unlinked from people.

Think of a stock market tape: everyone sees each trade, its time and its size, but not the names of the traders. That is Bitcoin's privacy model, and it ends the moment your name is attached to a key.

card.title: Privacy like a stock exchange tape
card.sub: Trades are public, traders are not. Once a key is tied to a person, privacy is gone.

long: The common-input-ownership heuristic is the base of chain analysis: when a transaction spends several inputs, they are assumed to belong to one owner, because each input needs a valid signature and one wallet normally signs them all. Applied transitively across many transactions, it merges addresses into clusters that likely belong to one entity, such as a person or an exchange.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #5: Common-input-ownership heuristic: all inputs of a transaction are assumed to share one owner, since each needs a valid signature and one wallet normally signs them all. It is the base of chain analysis.

Applied transitively across many transactions, it merges addresses into "clusters" that likely belong to one entity, such as a person or an exchange. Tracing tools start from these clusters.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #5: Rule #1 of blockchain tracing: if one payment spends coins from several addresses, tracers assume they belong to the same person, because one wallet usually signs them all.

Repeat this across thousands of payments and addresses snowball into big groups, each one likely a single person or company. That is how tracing tools build their map of who owns what.

card.title: Many inputs, one owner: the base rule
card.sub: Clustering co-spent inputs merges addresses into entities like people or exchanges.

long: A Bitcoin UTXO is spent whole, so a payment usually has a second output returning the leftover change to the sender at a new address. If an analyst can tell which output is change, using clues like round payment amounts, matching script types or a fresh never-seen address, they know which address still belongs to the sender. Meiklejohn et al. formalized change heuristics in 2013.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #6: Change-address heuristics: a UTXO is spent whole, so a payment usually has a second output returning the leftover to the sender at a new address. Spot the change, and you know which address is still the sender's.

Clues: round payment amounts, matching script types, or a fresh never-seen address. Meiklejohn et al. formalized these change heuristics in 2013, and tracing tools still use them.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #6: When you pay with Bitcoin, the leftover "change" goes back to a new address of yours, like change from a banknote. Spotting which output is the change tells a tracer which address is still you.

How do they guess? The payment is often a round number, the change is not. Or the change uses the same address type as your wallet. Small clues, but they add up fast.

card.title: Change outputs give the sender away
card.sub: Round amounts, matching scripts or fresh addresses reveal which output is change.

long: In "A Fistful of Bitcoins" (Meiklejohn et al., IMC 2013), researchers made 344 transactions with Bitcoin services to learn and tag their addresses. Combining those labels with the multi-input and change-address clustering heuristics, they could follow money flows to major exchanges and services. Commercial tracing firms scale up this same tag-and-cluster method.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #7: "A Fistful of Bitcoins" (Meiklejohn et al., IMC 2013): researchers made 344 transactions with Bitcoin services to tag their addresses, then used clustering to map money flows to exchanges and services.

They combined those labels with the multi-input and change-address heuristics. Commercial tracing firms now scale up this exact tag-and-cluster method across the whole chain.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #7: In 2013, researchers made 344 payments to Bitcoin services just to learn their addresses. With those few labels and the clustering tricks, they could follow money to big exchanges and services.

Today, tracing companies do the same thing on a massive scale: label known addresses, group the rest, and follow the flows. A few labels go a long way.

card.title: Tag a few addresses, trace the rest
card.sub: Researchers labeled services with test transactions, then followed flows to exchanges.

source: https://smeiklej.com/files/imc13.pdf (Meiklejohn et al., IMC 2013: 344 transactions with services to tag addresses, multi-input and change heuristics)

long: Reusing one address merges every payment into a single public record: balance, income and counterparties. Anyone who pays you or receives from you can see it all. HD wallets (BIP32) exist partly for this reason: they derive a fresh address for each receive. Reuse also gives analysts an anchor to cluster your other coins.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #8: Address reuse merges every payment into one public record: balance, income and counterparties. Anyone who pays you, or receives from you, can see all of it.

That's partly why HD wallets (BIP32) exist: they derive a fresh address for each receive. Reuse also gives analysts an anchor to cluster your other coins around one known address.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #8: Using the same address over and over is like handing everyone your bank statement. Anyone who pays you, or gets paid by you, can see your whole balance and history.

That's why modern wallets give you a new address every time you receive. It costs nothing and keeps each payment separate. Reusing one address also helps tracers find your other coins.

card.title: Address reuse builds a public profile
card.sub: Balance, income and counterparties land in one record. HD wallets use fresh addresses.

long: A dusting attack: an observer sends tiny amounts (dust) to many already-used addresses. If a wallet later spends that dust together with its other UTXOs in one transaction, the common-input heuristic links those addresses for the observer. Wallets with coin control can leave the dust unspent, which prevents the link.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #9: Dusting: an observer sends tiny outputs to many already-used addresses. If a wallet later co-spends that dust with its other UTXOs, the common-input heuristic links those addresses for the observer.

The defense is coin control: a wallet that lets you choose which coins to spend can leave the dust untouched. Unspent dust links nothing.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #9: A "dusting attack": someone sends tiny amounts of crypto to many addresses. If your wallet later spends that dust together with your other coins, it links your addresses for them.

It's a tracking trick, not a theft. Wallets with "coin control" let you choose which coins to spend, so you can simply leave the dust alone and the link never happens.

card.title: Dusting attacks bait your wallet
card.sub: Spend tiny dust with other coins and the addresses get linked. Coin control prevents it.

long: The usual weak point is not the blockchain but the on- and off-ramps. Exchanges that verify identity (KYC) link deposit and withdrawal addresses to real names in their records, and must answer subpoenas from authorities. A single KYC touchpoint can put a name on a whole cluster of addresses built with the clustering heuristics.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #10: On/off-ramps are the main deanonymization point: exchanges that verify identity (KYC) link deposit and withdrawal addresses to real names in their records, and must answer subpoenas.

Combined with clustering, a single KYC touchpoint can put a name on a whole cluster of addresses. The weak point is usually not the blockchain itself.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #10: The weakest link is usually not the blockchain, it's the exchange. Buy or sell on a platform that checked your ID, and your address is linked to your name in their records.

Authorities can ask the exchange for those records. And since tracers already group addresses into clusters, one linked address can put your name on many others.

card.title: Exchanges are the weak point
card.sub: One identity check can put a real name on a whole cluster of addresses.

long: Ledger data is public and permanent, so deanonymization works retroactively. A payment that looks untraceable today can be unmasked years later by new heuristics, a leaked database or a seized server. Example: the Bitfinex theft happened in 2016 and the arrests came in 2022. Privacy on a public chain has to hold forever, not just at the time of the payment.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #11: Ledger data is permanent and public, so deanonymization is retroactive: new heuristics, a leaked database or a seized server can unmask payments made years ago.

Example: the Bitfinex theft happened in 2016, and the arrests came in 2022. Privacy on a public chain has to hold forever, not just at the moment of the payment.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #11: The blockchain never forgets. A payment that looks untraceable today can be traced in 10 years with better tools or one leaked record. Privacy has to hold forever, not just today.

Real case: coins stolen from the Bitfinex exchange in 2016 led to arrests in 2022. Six years later, the same public records were still there to follow.

card.title: Deanonymization works years later
card.sub: The Bitfinex theft came first, the arrests six years on. Privacy has to hold forever.

long: Even without address links, amounts and timing leak. Unusual values, matching sums and tight time windows let analysts connect flows across hops, across chains and even through mixers. If 0.4271 BTC leaves one place and 0.4271 BTC appears elsewhere minutes later, an observer can connect the two. Analysts use this when address heuristics fail.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #12: Amount and timing correlation: odd values, matching sums and tight time windows link flows across hops, chains and even mixers. Analysts use it when address heuristics fail.

Example: if 0.4271 BTC leaves one place and 0.4271 BTC appears elsewhere minutes later, an observer can connect the two, even with no address link at all.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #12: Even without linking addresses, timing and amounts give you away. Send 0.4271 BTC and see 0.4271 BTC arrive somewhere minutes later: an observer can connect the two.

Unusual amounts and tight timing work like fingerprints. Tracers use them across hops, across chains, and even through mixers, when other clues run out.

card.title: Amounts and timing leak too
card.sub: Matching values in tight time windows connect flows across hops, chains and mixers.

long: Privacy can also leak at the network layer. Biryukov, Khovratovich and Pustogarov (CCS 2014) showed that a few machines connected to many Bitcoin nodes can link transactions to the IP addresses of the clients that broadcast them, even clients behind NAT. Nodes that hear a transaction first can guess where it came from.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #13: Network-layer deanonymization: Biryukov, Khovratovich & Pustogarov (CCS 2014) showed that a few machines connected to many Bitcoin nodes can link transactions to the IP addresses of the clients that sent them, even behind NAT.

The idea: nodes that hear a transaction first can guess where it came from. Privacy can leak below the blockchain, at the network layer.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #13: Your internet address can leak too. When your wallet broadcasts a payment, nodes that hear it first can guess where it came from, and link your address to your IP.

Researchers showed in 2014 that just a few machines connected to many Bitcoin nodes were enough to do this. The ledger is only one place where privacy can leak.

card.title: Your IP can betray your transaction
card.sub: A few well-connected machines can link transactions to the clients that broadcast them.

long: Light wallets need a server to find their transactions. BIP37 Bloom filters were meant to hide which addresses a client cares about, but Gervais et al. (2014) showed they leak a large share of a wallet's addresses to the node that answers. BIP157/158 compact block filters reverse the flow: the client downloads filters and checks them locally.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #14: BIP37 Bloom filters let light clients fetch their transactions without revealing exact addresses, but Gervais et al. (2014) showed they leak a large share of a wallet's addresses to the node that answers.

BIP157/158 compact block filters reverse the flow: the client downloads filters and checks them locally, so the server no longer learns which addresses it cares about.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #14: Light wallets on phones ask servers for their transactions. Early designs were meant to hide which addresses were yours, but researchers found they leaked many of them to whoever answered.

Newer designs flip it around: the wallet downloads a summary of each block and checks it on the phone itself. The server never learns what you were looking for.

card.title: Light wallets can leak your addresses
card.sub: BIP37 Bloom filters exposed many addresses. Compact filters are checked locally instead.

long: Ethereum uses an account model: one address holds a running balance, so most users reuse a single account for swaps, NFTs, salary and everything else. There is no fresh address per payment as in Bitcoin's UTXO wallets, so linking activity is often trivial. Token approvals and DeFi positions are public too, all on one page in a block explorer.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #15: Ethereum's account model: one address holds a running balance, so most users reuse a single account for everything. No fresh address per payment as in Bitcoin's UTXO wallets, so linking is often trivial.

Swaps, NFTs, salary: it's all one address. Token approvals and DeFi positions are public too, all on one page in a block explorer.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #15: Ethereum is even less private by default. Most people use one account for everything: swaps, NFTs, salary. Its whole history and balance sit on one public page.

Bitcoin wallets hand out a fresh address for each payment. Ethereum accounts usually don't, so there's nothing to link: it's already one address. Open a block explorer and it's all there.

card.title: One Ethereum account, one open book
card.sub: Swaps, NFTs, salary and token approvals all sit on a single public address page.

long: ENS maps readable names like alice.eth to addresses, and reverse records map addresses back to names, publicly on-chain. That makes payments easier but labels the wallet. If the name is also linked to a social profile, every transaction of that address carries a public identity anyone can look up.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #16: ENS maps readable names like alice.eth to addresses, and reverse records map addresses back to names, publicly on-chain. Convenient for payments, but it labels the wallet.

Link that name to a social profile and every transaction of that address carries a public identity. Anyone can look it up in a block explorer.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #16: A nice name like "alice.eth" makes payments easier, but it also puts a public label on your wallet. Anyone can look it up and see everything that address did.

If the same name is on your social profile, your whole on-chain history now has your face on it. Convenience and privacy pull in opposite directions here.

card.title: ENS names label your wallet
card.sub: Reverse records map addresses to names. Add a social profile and every payment is public.

long: On Nov 28, 2018, OFAC (US Treasury) listed digital currency addresses in a sanctions designation for the first time: two Iran-based individuals tied to exchanging SamSam ransomware payments. Addresses are now routinely added, and compliance tools screen transfers against them. This only works because blockchains are traceable.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #17: OFAC (US Treasury) first listed digital currency addresses in a sanctions designation on Nov 28, 2018: two Iran-based individuals tied to exchanging SamSam ransomware payments.

Addresses are now routinely added to sanctions lists, and compliance tools screen transfers against them. This only works because blockchains are traceable.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #17: Since 2018, the US sanctions list includes crypto addresses, not just names. Companies must block payments to them, which only works because blockchains are traceable.

The first case: two people in Iran tied to the SamSam ransomware. Today, compliance software checks transfers against these lists automatically.

card.title: First addresses on a US sanctions list
card.sub: OFAC listed two Iran-based individuals tied to SamSam ransomware payments.

long: Silk Road, the darknet market, ran on Bitcoin. Its founder Ross Ulbricht was arrested in Oct 2013, and the FBI seized about 144,000 BTC from his computer, then the largest Bitcoin seizure. The US Marshals later auctioned seized Silk Road coins in 2014-2015. Using Bitcoin did not hide him.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #18: Ross Ulbricht, founder of the Silk Road darknet market, was arrested in Oct 2013. The FBI seized ≈144,000 BTC from his computer, then the largest Bitcoin seizure.

The US Marshals later auctioned seized Silk Road coins in 2014-2015. The market ran on Bitcoin, and using Bitcoin did not hide its founder.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #18: Silk Road, the darknet market, ran on Bitcoin. When the FBI arrested its founder in 2013, it seized about 144,000 BTC from his laptop. Bitcoin didn't hide him.

At the time, it was the largest Bitcoin seizure ever. The US government later sold the seized coins at auctions in 2014 and 2015.

card.title: Silk Road's founder was not hidden
card.sub: The FBI seized the coins from Ross Ulbricht's computer, then the largest Bitcoin seizure.

long: In Nov 2020, seven years after Silk Road was shut down, the DOJ filed to forfeit about 69,370 BTC that a hacker, "Individual X", had stolen from the market. Investigators used blockchain analysis (Chainalysis) to trace the flows back to Silk Road's wallets. Old coins on a public ledger can still be followed.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #19: Nov 2020: the DOJ filed to forfeit ≈69,370 BTC stolen from Silk Road by a hacker known as "Individual X", seven years after the market was shut down.

Investigators used blockchain analysis (Chainalysis) to trace the flows back to Silk Road's wallets. Old coins on a public ledger can still be followed, years later.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #19: Seven years after Silk Road closed, the US traced and seized about 69,370 BTC that a hacker had stolen from it. Old coins, still followed.

Investigators used blockchain analysis to follow the money back to the market's wallets. The public ledger kept every step, waiting for someone to look.

card.title: Seven years later, the coins were traced
card.sub: Funds stolen by Individual X were followed back to Silk Road's wallets and forfeited.

long: James Zhong exploited Silk Road's withdrawal system in Sept 2012 and took over 50,000 BTC. In a Nov 2021 raid, agents found the coins in an underground floor safe and on a single-board computer hidden in a popcorn tin. He pleaded guilty in 2022. Nine years was not enough to stay hidden.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #20: James Zhong exploited Silk Road's withdrawal system in Sept 2012 to take 50,000+ BTC. A Nov 2021 raid found the coins in an underground floor safe and on a single-board computer hidden in a popcorn tin.

He pleaded guilty in 2022. Nine years between the theft and the raid was not enough to stay hidden.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #20: A man stole over 50,000 BTC from Silk Road in 2012 by tricking its withdrawal system. Agents found it in 2021, in a floor safe and on a tiny computer hidden in a popcorn tin.

He pleaded guilty in 2022. Nine years is a long time, but not long enough to hide on a ledger that never forgets.

card.title: Stolen bitcoin hidden in a popcorn tin
card.sub: James Zhong robbed Silk Road in 2012. Nine years later, agents found the coins.

long: In 2016, 119,754 BTC were stolen from the exchange Bitfinex. Investigators followed the coins for years. In Feb 2022, the DOJ arrested Ilya Lichtenstein and Heather Morgan and seized about 94,000 BTC, then worth about $3.6B, after tracing the funds through thousands of transactions to wallets they controlled.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #21: Bitfinex 2016: 119,754 BTC stolen. Feb 2022: the DOJ arrested Ilya Lichtenstein and Heather Morgan and seized ≈94,000 BTC, worth ≈$3.6B then.

Investigators followed the coins for years, tracing funds through thousands of transactions to wallets the two controlled.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #21: In 2016, hackers stole about 120,000 BTC from the exchange Bitfinex. Investigators followed the coins for years. In 2022: two arrests and about 94,000 BTC seized, then worth ≈$3.6B.

The money had gone through thousands of transactions. Every one was public, and investigators traced them all the way to wallets the suspects controlled.

card.title: The Bitfinex hack, traced for years
card.sub: In 2022 the DOJ seized about 94,000 BTC, then worth about $3.6B, from two suspects.

long: The Bitfinex launderers layered funds through many wallets, fake identities, chain-hopping, a darknet market and mixers. The trail still stayed on public ledgers. In Nov 2024, Ilya Lichtenstein was sentenced to 5 years in prison for the Bitfinex money laundering conspiracy.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #22: Ilya Lichtenstein was sentenced in Nov 2024 to 5 years for the Bitfinex money laundering conspiracy.

The layering was elaborate: many wallets, fake identities, chain-hopping, a darknet market and mixers. Yet the trail stayed on public ledgers throughout, and investigators followed it.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #22: The Bitfinex launderers used fake identities, chain-hopping and darknet services to hide the stolen coins. It didn't work: in Nov 2024 Ilya Lichtenstein was sentenced to 5 years for money laundering conspiracy.

Moving coins through many wallets and services adds steps, but each step stays on a public ledger. More steps mean more records, not fewer.

card.title: Layering did not erase the trail
card.sub: Mixers, fake identities and chain-hopping still left records on public ledgers.

long: In 2021, Colonial Pipeline paid a ransom in Bitcoin to the DarkSide ransomware group. In June 2021, the DOJ seized 63.7 BTC (about $2.3M) of it. Agents followed the transfers on Bitcoin's public ledger to an address whose private key the FBI held.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #23: Colonial Pipeline paid a ransom in Bitcoin to the DarkSide ransomware group in 2021. In June 2021 the DOJ seized 63.7 BTC (≈$2.3M) of it.

Agents traced the transfers on Bitcoin's public ledger to an address whose private key the FBI held, and took the coins back.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #23: 2021: Colonial Pipeline paid a ransom in Bitcoin to a ransomware gang. Weeks later, the FBI got most of it back by following the payment on the public ledger.

The trail led to a wallet whose key the FBI had. About 63.7 BTC, roughly $2.3M at the time, was seized. Ransom in Bitcoin is not a clean getaway.

card.title: Colonial Pipeline ransom partly recovered
card.sub: Agents followed the transfers to an address whose private key the FBI held.

long: Welcome To Video, a darknet child abuse site, took payment in Bitcoin; each user got a unique bitcoin address. Tracing those payments let investigators locate the server and its admin in South Korea. The DOJ announced in Oct 2019 that the case led to arrests of 337 users in the US and 11 other countries.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #24: Welcome To Video, a darknet child abuse site, gave each user a unique bitcoin address for payment. Tracing those payments located the server and its admin in South Korea.

The DOJ announced in Oct 2019 that the case led to the arrests of 337 users in the US and 11 other countries.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #24: A darknet abuse site took payment in Bitcoin, thinking it was untraceable. Tracing those payments led investigators to the site's server and its admin in South Korea.

In 2019, the US announced 337 arrests of users in 12 countries. Each user had paid to their own Bitcoin address, and those payments were all on the public ledger.

card.title: Unique addresses led to the server
card.sub: Tracing Welcome To Video payments located its admin in South Korea, then its users.

long: Hydra Market, the largest Russian-language darknet market, was taken down in April 2022: German authorities shut its servers and seized about $25M in bitcoin. The US Treasury sanctioned Hydra the same day, Apr 5, 2022, and listed more than 100 associated crypto addresses.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #25: Hydra Market takedown, Apr 2022: German authorities shut the servers of the largest Russian-language darknet market and seized ≈$25M in bitcoin.

The US Treasury sanctioned Hydra the same day, Apr 5, 2022, and listed 100+ associated crypto addresses, so compliance tools could flag them.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #25: Hydra, the biggest Russian-language darknet market, was taken down by German police in April 2022. They shut its servers and seized about $25M in bitcoin.

The same day, the US Treasury sanctioned Hydra and published more than 100 of its crypto addresses. Anyone dealing with them now gets flagged.

card.title: Hydra Market taken down
card.sub: Germany shut its servers; the US sanctioned it and listed over 100 crypto addresses.

long: On Feb 21, 2025, hackers stole about $1.5B in crypto, mostly ETH, from the exchange Bybit. On Feb 26, the FBI attributed the theft to North Korea's "TraderTraitor" activity and published Ethereum addresses holding the funds, asking exchanges, node operators and others to block transactions with them.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #26: Bybit hack, Feb 21, 2025: ≈$1.5B in crypto stolen, mostly ETH. On Feb 26, the FBI attributed it to North Korea's "TraderTraitor" activity and published Ethereum addresses holding the funds.

It asked exchanges, node operators and others to block transactions with those addresses. Five days from theft to public attribution.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #26: Feb 2025: hackers stole about $1.5B in crypto from the exchange Bybit. Within five days, the FBI named North Korea and published the addresses holding the funds.

It asked exchanges and others to block any transaction with them. Stolen coins on a public chain carry a label everyone can see.

card.title: FBI names North Korea in the Bybit hack
card.sub: It published addresses holding the stolen funds and asked exchanges to block them.

long: CoinJoin, named by Gregory Maxwell in 2013: several owners co-sign one combined transaction. Since the inputs no longer share one owner, it defeats the common-input heuristic, the base rule of tracing. Each participant signs only their own input after checking the outputs, so no one can steal the others' coins.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #27: CoinJoin, named by Gregory Maxwell in 2013: several owners co-sign one combined transaction. Inputs no longer share one owner, so it defeats the common-input heuristic, the base rule of tracing.

Each participant signs only their own input after checking the outputs, so no one can steal the others' coins. No trust in a third party is needed for that.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #27: CoinJoin: several people combine their payments into one big transaction. From outside, you can't tell whose coins went where, which breaks rule #1 of tracing.

And it's safe: each person checks the result and signs only their own part, so nobody can run off with someone else's coins. The idea was named in 2013.

card.title: CoinJoin breaks the common-input rule
card.sub: Several owners co-sign one transaction, and each signs only their own input.

long: In a CoinJoin, equal-value outputs form the anonymity set. With N identical outputs, such as 50 outputs of 0.1 BTC, amounts alone give only 1-in-N odds of matching an input to an output. Any leftover change output is not equal to the others, so it stays linkable to its input.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #28: In a CoinJoin, equal-value outputs form the anonymity set. With N identical outputs, such as 50 outputs of 0.1 BTC, amounts alone give only 1-in-N odds of matching an input to an output.

Any leftover change output is not equal to the others, so it stays linkable to its input. The anonymity set covers the equal outputs only.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #28: CoinJoin works best when everyone gets back the same amount, say 0.1 BTC each. With 50 identical outputs, each one could belong to any of the 50 participants.

But if you put in more than 0.1 BTC, your leftover comes back as a separate, different amount. That leftover is not hidden in the crowd and can still be linked to you.

card.title: Equal outputs form the anonymity set
card.sub: With identical outputs, amounts alone cannot match inputs. Leftover change stays linkable.

long: CoinJoin is not a magic eraser. Privacy depends on a coin's whole history: if mixed outputs are later spent together with change or unmixed coins, or merged with each other, the common-input heuristic links them again. Sending mixed coins straight to a KYC exchange can also tie them back to a person.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #29: CoinJoin gains are lost by post-mix mistakes. Privacy depends on a coin's whole history, not on one transaction.

Merging mixed outputs with change, with unmixed coins or with each other re-applies the common-input heuristic and links them again. Sending mixed coins straight to a KYC exchange can also tie them back to a person.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #29: CoinJoin isn't a magic eraser. If you later spend mixed and unmixed coins together, or send them straight to an exchange that knows you, you can link yourself back.

Privacy depends on everything that happens to a coin, before and after the mix. One careless payment can undo it.

card.title: CoinJoin is not a magic eraser
card.sub: Merging mixed coins with change, or sending them to a KYC exchange, can relink them.

long: JoinMarket, announced by Chris Belcher on Jan 9, 2015, turned CoinJoin into a market. "Makers" offer their coins as liquidity and earn fees; "takers" pay to build CoinJoins with them right away. There is no central coordinator, which matters given what later happened to coordinator-based services.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #30: JoinMarket, announced by Chris Belcher on Jan 9, 2015, turned CoinJoin into a market: "makers" offer their coins as liquidity and earn fees, "takers" pay to build CoinJoins with them right away.

There is no central coordinator, which matters given what later happened to coordinator-based services.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #30: JoinMarket (2015) turned CoinJoin into a market: some users offer their coins to mix and earn a small fee, others pay to mix right away.

There's no central server running it, just users finding each other. That detail turned out to matter: later, services built around a central coordinator ran into legal trouble.

card.title: JoinMarket turns mixing into a market
card.sub: Makers earn fees for liquidity, takers pay for instant CoinJoins. No central coordinator.

long: Wasabi Wallet 1.0 launched Oct 31, 2018 and made CoinJoin easy for non-experts; version 2.0 with the WabiSabi protocol came in June 2022. Its company zkSNACKs stopped its coinjoin coordinator on June 1, 2024, citing regulatory risk. The open-source wallet still works and can connect to other coordinators.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #31: Wasabi Wallet 1.0 launched Oct 31, 2018 and made CoinJoin easy for non-experts; 2.0 with the WabiSabi protocol came in June 2022.

Its company zkSNACKs stopped its coinjoin coordinator on June 1, 2024, citing regulatory risk. The open-source wallet still works and can connect to other coordinators.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #31: Wasabi Wallet made CoinJoin easy for everyone in 2018. In 2024, its company shut down its mixing server, citing legal uncertainty. The wallet remained, the main coordinator went away.

Because the wallet is open source, it still works and can connect to other coordinators. But the default, one-click option is gone.

card.title: Wasabi's coordinator went dark in 2024
card.sub: zkSNACKs cited regulatory risk. The open-source wallet can still use other coordinators.

long: Samourai Wallet ran a CoinJoin service called Whirlpool. Founders Keonne Rodriguez and William Hill were charged in 2024 and sentenced in Nov 2025 to 5 and 4 years for running an unlicensed money transmitting business. The DOJ says over 80,000 BTC passed through Whirlpool and Ricochet, including over $237M of criminal proceeds.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #32: Samourai Wallet ran the Whirlpool CoinJoin service. Founders Keonne Rodriguez and William Hill were charged in 2024 and sentenced in Nov 2025 to 5 and 4 years for running an unlicensed money transmitting business.

The DOJ says over 80,000 BTC passed through Whirlpool and Ricochet, including over $237M of criminal proceeds.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #32: Samourai Wallet ran a CoinJoin service called Whirlpool. Its founders were charged in 2024 and sentenced in Nov 2025 to 5 and 4 years for running an unlicensed money business.

US prosecutors say more than 80,000 BTC went through its services, including over $237M linked to crime. Running the mixer, not just using it, carried the risk.

card.title: Samourai founders sentenced
card.sub: The DOJ says over 80,000 BTC passed through Whirlpool and Ricochet.

long: PayJoin (BIP78): when paying a receiver, such as a shop, the receiver adds one of its own inputs to the transaction. It looks like an ordinary payment, but the common-input heuristic now wrongly merges sender and receiver, and the receiver's output no longer equals the amount paid, which misleads amount analysis.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #33: PayJoin (BIP78): when paying a receiver such as a shop, the receiver adds one of its own inputs to the transaction. It looks like an ordinary payment.

But the common-input heuristic now wrongly merges sender and receiver, and the receiver's output no longer equals the amount paid, which misleads amount analysis.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #33: PayJoin: when you pay a shop, the shop adds one of its own coins to your transaction. It looks like a normal payment, but rule #1 of tracing now points the wrong way.

A tracer would assume all the coins are yours, which is false. And the amount the shop receives no longer matches the price, so amount analysis gets confused too.

card.title: PayJoin fools the analysts
card.sub: The receiver adds an input, so tracing wrongly merges sender and receiver.

long: Taproot (BIPs 340-342) activated in Nov 2021 at block 709,632. With a key-path spend, an output controlled by a multisig or a contract looks like an ordinary single-key Schnorr payment, and unused script branches are never revealed. In the common case, complex wallets give fewer clues to trackers.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #34: Taproot (BIPs 340-342) activated in Nov 2021 at block 709,632. With a key-path spend, a multisig or contract output looks like an ordinary single-key Schnorr payment.

Unused script branches are never revealed. In the common case, complex wallets give trackers fewer clues about how they are set up.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #34: Bitcoin's 2021 Taproot upgrade made complex wallets, like shared or multi-signature ones, look like normal single wallets on-chain in the common case. Fewer clues for trackers.

Before, a special wallet stood out by its shape. Now, as long as everyone agrees, it looks like any other payment, and the hidden backup rules are never shown.

card.title: Taproot makes complex wallets look plain
card.sub: Multisig and contract outputs can pass as ordinary single-key Schnorr payments.

source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bitcoin/bips/master/bip-0341.mediawiki (Deployment: "deployed concurrently with BIP342", "did activate at height 709632") + https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bitcoin/bips/master/bip-0342.mediawiki ("deployed identically to Taproot") + https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bitcoinops/bitcoinops.github.io/master/_posts/en/newsletters/2021-11-17-newsletter.md (Optech, Nov 17, 2021: "Taproot activated")

long: Lightning payments are not recorded on the Bitcoin blockchain one by one. They are routed with onion routing (Sphinx), so each hop knows only the previous and next node. Channel opens and closes are on-chain and public. The spec itself warns that traffic analysis can still link payments.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #35: Lightning payments aren't recorded on-chain one by one. They use onion routing (Sphinx): each hop knows only the previous and next node.

Channel opens and closes are on-chain and public, though. And the spec itself warns that traffic analysis can still link payments, so Lightning is more private, not invisible.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #35: Lightning payments don't go on the Bitcoin blockchain one by one, and they hop through several nodes like a relay. Each node only sees the one before and the one after.

Opening and closing a channel is still public on-chain. And the Lightning spec itself warns that watching traffic can still link payments. Better privacy, not perfect.

card.title: Lightning keeps payments off-chain
card.sub: Onion routing hides the path, but channel opens and closes are public on-chain.

long: A custodial mixer pools deposits in its own wallet and pays out different coins, minus a fee. Unlike CoinJoin, the operator holds the funds and keeps the full map of who sent what and who got what. Users must trust it not to steal, and a leak or seizure of its records can expose them.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #36: Custodial mixers take deposits into a pooled wallet and pay out other coins, minus a fee. Unlike CoinJoin, the operator holds the funds and keeps the full map of who sent what and who got what.

Users must trust it not to steal, and a leak or seizure of its records can expose every user at once.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #36: A custodial "mixer" works like a coin swap counter: you hand over coins and get different ones back, minus a fee. You must trust the operator not to steal, and to keep secret who got what.

Unlike CoinJoin, the operator holds everything and knows everything. If its records leak or police seize its servers, all its users can be exposed.

card.title: Custodial mixers keep the full map
card.sub: The operator holds the funds and knows who sent what. A seizure can expose users.

long: Bitcoin Fog was one of the oldest mixers, running from 2011 to 2021. The DOJ says it moved over 1.2M BTC, about $400M at the time, much of it from darknet markets. Its operator Roman Sterlingov was sentenced on Nov 8, 2024 to 12 years and 6 months in prison.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #37: Bitcoin Fog, one of the oldest mixers, ran from 2011 to 2021. The DOJ says it moved over 1.2M BTC, ≈$400M at the time, much of it from darknet markets.

Its operator Roman Sterlingov was sentenced on Nov 8, 2024 to 12 years and 6 months in prison. Ten years of operation, then a long sentence.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #37: Bitcoin Fog was one of the oldest mixers, running from 2011 to 2021. Its operator was sentenced in Nov 2024 to 12.5 years in prison.

US prosecutors say it moved over 1.2 million BTC, about $400M at the time, much of it from darknet markets. A decade of mixing did not make its operator untraceable.

card.title: One of the oldest mixers, shut down
card.sub: Bitcoin Fog moved over 1.2M BTC. Its operator got 12 years and 6 months.

long: Helix was a bitcoin mixer run from 2014 to 2017 and tied to Grams, a darknet market search engine. The DOJ says it moved about 354,000 BTC, worth about $300M at the time. Operator Larry Harmon pleaded guilty and was sentenced in Nov 2024 to 3 years for a money laundering conspiracy.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #38: Helix (2014-2017) was a bitcoin mixer tied to Grams, a darknet market search engine. The DOJ says it moved ≈354,000 BTC, worth ≈$300M at the time.

Operator Larry Harmon pleaded guilty and was sentenced in Nov 2024 to 3 years for a money laundering conspiracy. Mixing customers' coins did not keep the operator hidden.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #38: Helix was a bitcoin mixer built into Grams, a darknet market search engine. Its operator pleaded guilty and in Nov 2024 was sentenced to 3 years in prison.

It ran from 2014 to 2017 and, according to US prosecutors, moved about 354,000 BTC, worth about $300M at the time. The coins were mixed, but the operator was still found.

card.title: Helix mixer tied to a darknet search engine
card.sub: Operator Larry Harmon pleaded guilty and got 3 years for money laundering conspiracy.

long: On Mar 15, 2023, German and US authorities, supported by Europol, took down the ChipMixer service. They seized 4 servers and about 1,909 BTC (about EUR 44M). ChipMixer allegedly mixed about 152,000 BTC, including ransomware payments.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #39: ChipMixer takedown, Mar 15, 2023: German and US authorities, supported by Europol, seized 4 servers and ≈1,909 BTC (≈€44M).

ChipMixer allegedly mixed ≈152,000 BTC, including ransomware payments. Seized servers also mean seized records of who used the service.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #39: March 2023: German and US police, with Europol's help, shut down the ChipMixer service and seized about €44M in bitcoin from it.

They also took its servers. The service is accused of mixing about 152,000 BTC, including ransomware payments. A mixer that keeps records is a mixer that can be read.

card.title: ChipMixer taken down
card.sub: German and US authorities seized 4 servers. It allegedly mixed about 152,000 BTC.

long: On May 6, 2022, OFAC sanctioned Blender.io, its first ever designation of a virtual currency mixer. It cited the mixer's use by North Korea's Lazarus Group to launder proceeds of the Ronin bridge hack (Axie Infinity).
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #40: OFAC sanctioned Blender.io on May 6, 2022, its first ever designation of a virtual currency mixer.

It cited the mixer's use by North Korea's Lazarus Group to launder proceeds of the Ronin bridge hack (Axie Infinity). Sanctioning a mixer means US persons and firms must not deal with it.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #40: In May 2022, Blender.io became the first crypto mixer ever sanctioned by the US Treasury, for helping North Korean hackers launder stolen funds.

The money came from the hack of the Ronin bridge, used by the game Axie Infinity. After the sanction, US people and companies could no longer deal with the mixer.

card.title: Blender.io, the first sanctioned mixer
card.sub: OFAC cited its use by Lazarus Group to launder Ronin bridge hack proceeds.

long: When one mixer closes, another appears. On Nov 29, 2023, OFAC sanctioned the mixer Sinbad.io, the same day its website was seized. Analysts at Elliptic had linked it to Blender.io as a likely successor, and it was used by North Korea's Lazarus Group.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #41: OFAC sanctioned the mixer Sinbad.io on Nov 29, 2023, the same day its website was seized.

Analysts at Elliptic had linked it to Blender.io as a likely successor, and it was used by North Korea's Lazarus Group. When one mixer closes, another tends to appear, and gets tracked in turn.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #41: When one mixer is closed, another appears. In Nov 2023 the US sanctioned Sinbad, a mixer seen as Blender.io's successor, also used by North Korean hackers.

Its website was seized the same day. Analysts had connected it to Blender.io by studying the flows. Even the successor of a sanctioned mixer leaves a trail.

card.title: Sinbad.io, a likely Blender.io successor
card.sub: OFAC sanctioned it the same day its website was seized. Lazarus Group used it too.

long: Tornado Cash on Ethereum: a user deposits a fixed amount with a secret commitment, then later withdraws to a fresh address using a zk-SNARK proving they own an unspent deposit in the pool, without revealing which one. All deposits of the same size in the pool form the anonymity set.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #42: Tornado Cash on Ethereum: deposit a fixed amount with a secret commitment, then later withdraw to a fresh address with a zk-SNARK proving you own an unspent deposit in the pool, without revealing which one.

All deposits of the same size in the pool form the anonymity set. The bigger the pool, the harder it is to match a withdrawal to a deposit.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #42: Tornado Cash works like a sealed box: people drop in fixed amounts of ETH, then later take them out to a new address, proving they deposited without saying which deposit.

The proof uses zero-knowledge math. Everyone who put in the same amount is a possible match, so the more people use the box, the better it hides each one.

card.title: How Tornado Cash hides the link
card.sub: A zk-SNARK proves you own a deposit in the pool without revealing which one.

long: On Aug 8, 2022, OFAC designated Tornado Cash and listed its smart contract addresses. Treasury said it had laundered more than $7B since 2019, including over $455M stolen by North Korea's Lazarus Group. It was the first sanction of immutable, open-source code.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #43: OFAC designated Tornado Cash on Aug 8, 2022, listing its smart contract addresses. Treasury said it had laundered $7B+ since 2019, including $455M+ stolen by North Korea's Lazarus Group.

It was the first sanction of immutable, open-source code: not a company or a person, but contracts that nobody could switch off.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #43: Aug 2022: the US Treasury sanctioned Tornado Cash, saying it had laundered more than $7B since 2019, including over $455M stolen by North Korean hackers.

It was a first: the sanction targeted open-source code running on Ethereum, not a company or a person. Nobody could switch that code off, which raised a big legal question.

card.title: Sanctions hit open-source code
card.sub: OFAC listed its contracts, citing over $455M stolen by North Korea's Lazarus Group.

long: Can code nobody controls be sanctioned? In Van Loon v. Treasury (Nov 26, 2024), the US Fifth Circuit ruled that Tornado Cash's immutable smart contracts are not "property" under IEEPA, so OFAC cannot block them. Treasury delisted Tornado Cash on Mar 21, 2025.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #44: Van Loon v. Treasury (5th Cir., Nov 26, 2024): Tornado Cash's immutable smart contracts aren't "property" under IEEPA, so OFAC can't block them.

Treasury then delisted Tornado Cash on Mar 21, 2025. The ruling is about the immutable contracts, not about the people who use or build them.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #44: Can you sanction code nobody controls? A US appeals court said no in Nov 2024: code that nobody can change or own is not "property" that can be blocked.

In March 2025, the Treasury removed Tornado Cash from its sanctions list. That answered the code question in that case, but not the cases against its developers.

card.title: A court says code is not property
card.sub: The Fifth Circuit ruled OFAC cannot block immutable contracts. Treasury then delisted it.

long: On May 14, 2024, a Dutch court in 's-Hertogenbosch convicted Tornado Cash developer Alexey Pertsev of money laundering and sentenced him to 64 months. He appealed. The case is a key test of whether writing privacy software can make a developer liable.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #45: May 14, 2024: a court in 's-Hertogenbosch (Netherlands) convicted Tornado Cash developer Alexey Pertsev of money laundering and sentenced him to 64 months.

He appealed. The case is a key test of whether writing privacy software can make a developer liable for what others do with it.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #45: Writing privacy code can still land you in court. In May 2024, a Dutch court sentenced Tornado Cash developer Alexey Pertsev to 64 months for money laundering.

He appealed. The case matters far beyond him: it tests whether a developer can be blamed for how other people use the software they wrote.

card.title: A Dutch court convicts a privacy developer
card.sub: Tornado Cash developer Alexey Pertsev was found guilty of money laundering. He appealed.

long: In the US, Tornado Cash co-founder Roman Storm went on trial in 2025. In Aug 2025 in SDNY, the jury convicted him of conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business, and deadlocked on the money laundering and sanctions conspiracy charges.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #46: Aug 2025, SDNY: Tornado Cash co-founder Roman Storm was convicted of conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business.

The jury deadlocked on the money laundering and sanctions conspiracy charges. The US and Dutch cases together show developers of privacy tools facing real legal risk.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #46: In the US, Tornado Cash co-founder Roman Storm went on trial in 2025. In August, the jury found him guilty on one charge: running an unlicensed money transmitting business.

It couldn't agree on the other charges, money laundering and sanctions. Along with the Dutch case, it shows that building privacy tools carries legal risk.

card.title: Roman Storm's split verdict
card.sub: Convicted of unlicensed money transmitting conspiracy; jury deadlocked on other charges.

long: Monero was designed to hide what Bitcoin leaves public, and its privacy is on by default: ring signatures hide which input is real (the sender), one-time stealth addresses hide the receiver, and RingCT hides amounts. Since privacy is mandatory, all users share one large anonymity set instead of a small opt-in group.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #47: Monero's privacy stack is on by default: ring signatures hide the real input (the sender), one-time stealth addresses hide the receiver, RingCT hides amounts.

Because privacy is mandatory, all users share one large anonymity set instead of a small opt-in group, which is a weak point of optional privacy.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #47: Monero was built to fix what Bitcoin leaves open. It hides three things by default: who sent, who received, and how much. Not optional, for everyone.

That last part matters. When privacy is optional, the few who use it stand out. When everyone has it, each user hides among all the others.

card.title: Monero: private by default
card.sub: Ring signatures, stealth addresses and RingCT hide sender, receiver and amount.

long: Monero uses CLSAG ring signatures: each input is signed with a ring of 16 members, 1 real and 15 decoys, and observers cannot tell which is real. Ring size became 16 with the v0.18 hard fork in Aug 2022. Key images prevent double spends without revealing the signer.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #48: Monero ring signatures (CLSAG): each input is signed with a ring of 16 members, 1 real + 15 decoys, and observers can't tell which is real. Ring size became 16 in the v0.18 hard fork (Aug 2022).

Key images prevent double spends: the same output can't be spent twice, yet the key image doesn't reveal which ring member signed.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #48: In Monero, each payment is signed by a group of 16 possible senders. Only one is real, and nobody watching can tell which. That's a ring signature.

The other 15 are decoys taken from the blockchain. A clever tag still stops anyone from spending the same coin twice, without revealing who the real signer was.

card.title: Hiding the real signer among decoys
card.sub: Each input has 15 decoys; key images stop double spends without naming the signer.

long: Monero stealth addresses: a user shares one public address, but for each payment the sender derives a one-time output key from the recipient's public view and spend keys plus random data. Only sender and recipient can link it; the recipient finds it by scanning with the private view key. Outsiders can't tie payments together.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #49: Monero stealth addresses: the sender derives a one-time output key from the recipient's public view and spend keys plus random data. Only sender and recipient can link it to the recipient.

The recipient finds it by scanning the chain with the private view key. Outsiders see unrelated one-time keys and can't tie payments together.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #49: In Monero, you can share one public address, yet every payment you receive lands at a brand new one-time address. Outsiders can't tie your payments together.

Your wallet scans the blockchain with a special key to find what's yours. To everyone else, your payments look like unrelated strangers.

card.title: One public address, endless one-time keys
card.sub: Each payment gets a fresh output key that only sender and recipient can link.

long: RingCT, mandatory in Monero since 2017, hides amounts with Pedersen commitments, and range proofs show amounts are not negative, so the network can check no coins are created from nothing. Bulletproofs (Oct 2018) shrank those proofs, and Bulletproofs+ (Aug 2022) cut size and verification time again.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #50: RingCT (mandatory in Monero since 2017) hides amounts with Pedersen commitments; range proofs show amounts aren't negative, so the network can check no coins are created from nothing.

Bulletproofs (Oct 2018) shrank those proofs, and Bulletproofs+ (Aug 2022) cut size and verification time again.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #50: Monero also hides amounts. The network can still check that no coins were created from nothing, without anyone seeing how much was sent.

The trick is a math proof that the hidden numbers add up and none is negative. Since 2018, upgrades have made those proofs much smaller and faster to check.

card.title: Hidden amounts that still add up
card.sub: Pedersen commitments hide values, while range proofs show no coins are created.

long: Privacy doesn't rule out disclosure. A Monero wallet has a private view key, separate from the spend key. Sharing the view key gives read-only access to incoming outputs, for an auditor, accountant or tax office, without any power to spend. Outgoing payments can't be reliably seen with it alone.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #51: Monero wallets have a private view key, separate from the spend key. Sharing it gives read-only access to incoming outputs, for an auditor, accountant or tax office, with no power to spend.

Outgoing payments can't be reliably seen with the view key alone. Privacy by default, disclosure by choice.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #51: Private doesn't mean you can't show anything. A Monero "view key" lets you give an auditor, accountant or tax office read-only access to your incoming payments.

They can see what came in, but they can't move a single coin. You decide who gets to look, instead of the whole world seeing everything by default.

card.title: A view key for auditors, not spenders
card.sub: It shows incoming outputs read-only, with no power to spend. Outgoing stays unclear.

long: Monero added Dandelion++ in v0.16 (2020). A new transaction first goes through a "stem" phase, forwarded along a random path of single peers, then a "fluff" phase floods it to the network. This makes the original broadcaster hard to spot and weakens the IP-linking attacks that work on plain gossip networks.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #52: Dandelion++ (added in Monero v0.16, 2020): a new tx first goes through a "stem" phase, forwarded along a random path of single peers, then a "fluff" phase floods it to the network.

This makes the original broadcaster hard to spot and weakens the IP-linking attacks that work on plain gossip networks.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #52: Monero also hides where a transaction starts on the internet. It's passed quietly from node to node first, then spread widely, so the first broadcaster is hard to spot.

On a normal network, the nodes that hear a payment first can guess its origin. This two-step relay makes that guess much harder.

card.title: Dandelion++ hides who broadcast first
card.sub: A random stem path, then a flood, weakens IP-linking attacks on Monero.

long: Monero's early privacy was weaker. Möser et al. (PoPETs 2018) found that about 62% of early inputs with mixins could be deduced by chain-reaction analysis, and that guessing the newest ring member was right about 80% of the time, mostly due to weak decoys. Bigger rings and better decoy selection followed.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #53: Möser et al. (PoPETs 2018): ≈62% of early Monero inputs with mixins could be deduced by chain-reaction analysis, and guessing the newest ring member was right ≈80% of the time.

The main cause was weak decoys. Bigger rings and better decoy selection followed. Privacy protocols harden over time.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #53: Monero wasn't always this strong. A 2018 study found that in its early years, many payments could be traced, mostly because the decoys were easy to tell apart from the real sender.

Often, the real coin was simply the newest one in the group. Monero then made rings bigger and picked decoys better.

card.title: Early Monero privacy was weaker
card.sub: Guessing the newest ring member was right about 80% of the time, due to weak decoys.

long: In Sept 2020, the IRS awarded contracts to Chainalysis and Integra FEC, up to $625K each and $1.25M in total, to build Monero tracing tools. No public break of Monero's cryptography, or general method to trace it, has been shown.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #54: Sept 2020: the IRS awarded contracts to Chainalysis and Integra FEC, up to $625K each and $1.25M in total, to build Monero tracing tools.

No public break of Monero's cryptography, or general method to trace it, has been shown since. A contract to try is not proof of success.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #54: Can governments crack Monero? In 2020, the US tax agency paid two firms up to $1.25M in total to try to build Monero tracing tools.

So far, no public proof of a general break has been shown, and no general method to trace it has been published. Paying someone to try is not the same as succeeding.

card.title: The IRS paid for Monero tracing tools
card.sub: No public break of Monero's cryptography, or general method to trace it, has been shown.

long: Privacy coins pay a price in access: major exchanges remove them. Binance, the largest exchange, delisted XMR on Feb 20, 2024, after first adding a monitoring tag. Other exchanges in several jurisdictions have done the same, because default-private coins conflict with AML and Travel Rule obligations.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #55: Binance, the largest exchange, delisted XMR on Feb 20, 2024, after first adding a monitoring tag.

Other exchanges in several jurisdictions have done the same, because default-private coins conflict with AML and Travel Rule obligations. Privacy coins pay a price in access.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #55: Privacy coins have a cost: big exchanges remove them. Binance, the largest one, delisted Monero in Feb 2024, after first flagging it for monitoring.

Other exchanges in several countries did the same. Rules against money laundering require them to know who sends what, and a coin private by default makes that hard.

card.title: Privacy coins lose exchange access
card.sub: Binance delisted XMR in 2024, as default privacy clashes with AML and Travel Rule duties.

long: Zcash launched on Oct 28, 2016 (genesis block), built on the Zerocash protocol. Its shielded transactions use zk-SNARKs, proofs that inputs are valid and balanced, while sender, receiver and amount stay encrypted on-chain. It is a different route to privacy than Monero's decoys.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #56: Zcash launched Oct 28, 2016 (genesis block), built on the Zerocash protocol. Shielded transactions use zk-SNARKs to prove inputs are valid and balanced.

Sender, receiver and amount stay encrypted on-chain. It is a different route to privacy than Monero's decoys: proofs instead of crowds.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #56: Zcash takes another route: for shielded payments, math proves a payment is valid without showing who paid, who got paid, or how much. It launched in 2016.

Monero hides the real sender among decoys. Zcash shielded payments encrypt everything and attach a proof that the payment adds up. Two different ideas for the same goal.

card.title: Zcash encrypts the whole transaction
card.sub: zk-SNARKs prove validity while sender, receiver and amount stay encrypted on-chain.

long: A zero-knowledge proof convinces a verifier that a statement is true, such as "I own an unspent note in this set", while revealing nothing else, like proving you are over 18 without showing your birth date. zk-SNARKs are short and fast to verify, which makes them usable on-chain. They power Zcash and Tornado Cash.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #57: A zero-knowledge proof convinces a verifier that a statement is true, e.g. "I own an unspent note in this set", while revealing nothing else.

zk-SNARKs are short and fast to verify, which makes them usable on-chain. They power Zcash shielded payments and Tornado Cash withdrawals.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #57: Zero-knowledge proof: proving you know a secret without revealing it. Like proving you're over 18 without showing your birth date.

The proofs used in crypto are tiny and quick to check, which is why they fit on a blockchain. They are the engine behind Zcash and Tornado Cash.

card.title: Proving a fact without revealing it
card.sub: Like showing you are over 18 without your birth date. zk-SNARKs make it fit on-chain.

long: Zcash privacy is optional. It has transparent t-addresses that work like Bitcoin's public UTXOs, and separate shielded pools. Kappos et al. (USENIX Security 2018) showed that simple heuristics based on usage patterns considerably shrink the shielded anonymity set.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #58: Zcash privacy is optional: transparent t-addresses work like Bitcoin's public UTXOs, next to separate shielded pools.

Kappos et al. (USENIX Security 2018) showed that simple heuristics based on usage patterns considerably shrink the shielded anonymity set. Optional privacy is only as strong as how people use it.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #58: Myth: "Zcash is always private." Privacy is optional. Its transparent addresses work like Bitcoin's, public for all.

A 2018 study showed that simple patterns, like coins going in and out of the private pool in the same amounts, could shrink its privacy a lot. Private tools still need private habits.

card.title: Optional privacy shrinks the crowd
card.sub: Usage-pattern heuristics considerably shrink Zcash's shielded anonymity set.

long: Zcash usage has moved toward privacy. In Oct 2025, the shielded supply (Sapling + Orchard pools) reached about 4.5M ZEC, a record at the time, driven in part by wallets that shield by default. A bigger shielded pool means a bigger anonymity set for every user in it.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #59: Zcash usage has moved toward privacy: the shielded supply (Sapling + Orchard pools) reached ≈4.5M ZEC in late Oct 2025.

Wallets that make shielding easy drove part of it. A bigger shielded pool means a bigger anonymity set for every user in it, though usage patterns can still shrink it in practice.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #59: Zcash usage has shifted toward privacy. In Oct 2025, about 4.5 million ZEC sat in its private, shielded pools.

Part of the reason: wallets that make the private option easy to use. And the more coins in the private pool, the better each user can hide in it.

card.title: Zcash's shielded supply reached a record
card.sub: Wallets that shield by default helped. A bigger pool means a bigger anonymity set.

long: Zcash's original SNARKs needed a trusted setup: a ceremony whose secret leftovers ("toxic waste") had to be destroyed. The NU5 upgrade on May 31, 2022 added the Orchard shielded pool, built on Halo 2, which needs no trusted setup.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #60: Zcash's original SNARKs needed a trusted setup: a ceremony whose secret leftovers ("toxic waste") had to be destroyed, or fake coins could be minted undetected.

The NU5 upgrade (May 31, 2022) added the Orchard shielded pool, built on Halo 2, which needs no trusted setup.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #60: Zcash's early design needed a secret setup ceremony whose leftovers had to be destroyed. If they had survived, someone could have created coins out of nothing, unseen.

A 2022 upgrade added a new private pool built on newer math that needs no ceremony at all. One big trust assumption, removed.

card.title: Goodbye to the toxic waste ceremony
card.sub: The NU5 upgrade added Orchard, built on Halo 2, which needs no trusted setup.

long: Zcash supports viewing keys (ZIP 310). An incoming or full viewing key reveals a shielded address's transactions without giving spend authority. This enables selective disclosure, for audits or compliance, while staying private toward everyone else, similar to Monero's view key.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #61: Zcash viewing keys (ZIP 310): an incoming or full viewing key reveals a shielded address's transactions without spend authority.

This enables selective disclosure for audits and compliance, while staying private toward everyone else, similar to Monero's view key.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #61: Like Monero, Zcash lets you share a viewing key, so an auditor can see your shielded payments without being able to spend your coins.

You can show your accountant or a regulator exactly what they need, and stay private toward everyone else. Privacy and accountability don't have to be opposites.

card.title: Viewing keys for selective disclosure
card.sub: They reveal a shielded address's transactions without granting spend authority.

long: Privacy Pools (2023 paper co-written by Vitalik Buterin): users prove with a zero-knowledge proof that their deposit belongs to an approved "association set" that excludes known illicit deposits, without revealing which deposit is theirs. The aim is privacy plus a way to show funds are not from a known bad source.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #62: Privacy Pools (2023 paper co-written by Vitalik Buterin): users prove with a zero-knowledge proof that their deposit belongs to an approved "association set" excluding known illicit deposits.

They do so without revealing which deposit is theirs. The aim: privacy, plus a way to show funds are not from a known bad source.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #62: Can you have privacy and still prove your money is clean? A 2023 paper co-written by Vitalik Buterin proposed "Privacy Pools": prove your funds aren't from a known bad source.

You don't reveal which deposit is yours. You only prove it belongs to a group that excludes known stolen or criminal funds.

card.title: Prove clean funds, keep your privacy
card.sub: A zero-knowledge proof shows a deposit sits in an approved set, without saying which.

long: Banks pass sender and receiver details along with wire transfers. In 2019, the FATF, the global AML standard setter, extended Recommendation 16, the "Travel Rule", to virtual asset service providers: originator and beneficiary information must travel with transfers between VASPs. The EU applies it from the first euro.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #63: FATF (2019) extended Recommendation 16, the "Travel Rule", to virtual asset service providers: originator and beneficiary information must travel with transfers between VASPs, as with bank wires.

The EU applies it from the first euro. Exchanges now pass customer data to each other along with the coins.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #63: Banks share sender and receiver names when they wire money. Since 2019, the global anti-money-laundering standard asks crypto exchanges to do the same.

It's called the "Travel Rule": the identity data travels with the transfer. In the EU, it applies to every transfer between platforms, from the very first euro.

card.title: The Travel Rule comes to crypto
card.sub: Since 2019, originator and beneficiary data must travel with transfers between VASPs.

long: The EU AML Regulation 2024/1624, Art. 79, applying from July 10, 2027, bars crypto-asset service providers from keeping anonymous accounts, or accounts that allow transactions to be obfuscated, "including through anonymity-enhancing coins". The text names no coin; Monero (XMR) and Zcash (ZEC) are commonly cited examples.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #64: EU AMLR 2024/1624, Art. 79, applying from July 10, 2027: crypto-asset service providers may not keep anonymous accounts, or accounts that allow transactions to be obfuscated, "including through anonymity-enhancing coins".

The text names no coin; Monero (XMR) and Zcash (ZEC) are commonly cited examples.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #64: Europe is closing the door on anonymous crypto accounts. From July 2027, regulated crypto platforms in the EU may not offer anonymous accounts, or accounts that hide transactions with privacy coins.

The law doesn't name specific coins, but Monero and Zcash are the examples most often cited.

card.title: The EU bans anonymous crypto accounts
card.sub: Providers must not keep accounts that allow obfuscation, including via privacy coins.

long: Is crypto mostly for crime? Chainalysis's 2026 report (Jan 2026) estimates illicit addresses received a record $154B in 2025, a lower bound, mainly driven by sanctioned entities and state-level sanctions evasion. The 2024 figure was revised to $57.2B from $40.9B first reported. Illicit activity is still under 1% of on-chain volume. Public ledgers are what make such counts possible.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #65: Chainalysis 2026 report (Jan 2026): illicit addresses received ≈$154B in 2025, a record and a lower bound, driven mainly by sanctioned entities and state-level sanctions evasion.

The 2024 figure was revised to $57.2B from $40.9B first reported. Illicit activity is still under 1% of on-chain volume. Public ledgers make such counts possible.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #65: Myth: "crypto is mostly for crime." Chainalysis estimates illicit addresses got at least ≈$154B in 2025, a record driven by sanctions evasion, yet still under 1% of all on-chain volume.

And note how we know: these numbers can only be counted because blockchains are public. Cash crime leaves no such ledger.

card.title: Is crypto mostly for crime?
card.sub: Illicit activity is still under 1% of on-chain volume. Public ledgers make it countable.

long: On-chain privacy has legitimate uses. On a public ledger, competitors can see salaries and supplier payments, thieves can see balances, and hostile regimes can see donations. For a person, a shop or an employer, that is a real risk. This is why selective disclosure tools exist: view keys and zero-knowledge proofs let users show what they choose to the people they choose.
tech:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #66: Legit reasons for on-chain privacy: on a public ledger, competitors can see salaries and supplier payments, thieves can see balances, hostile regimes can see donations.

For a person, a shop or an employer, that's a real risk. Hence selective disclosure tools: view keys and ZK proofs show what you choose, to whom you choose.
simple:
Crypto #Anonymity Myths #66: Privacy isn't only for criminals. If your wallet is public, anyone you pay can see your salary, savings and spending. For an employer, a shop or a family, that's a real risk.

Thieves can see who holds a lot. Hostile governments can see who donated. That's why tools exist to share only what you choose, with the people you choose.

card.title: Why honest users want privacy
card.sub: Public ledgers show salaries, balances and donations to competitors, thieves and regimes.

long: Recap: Bitcoin is pseudonymous, not anonymous. Public ledgers plus clustering heuristics plus KYC records make flows traceable, even years later, as Silk Road, Bitfinex and Colonial Pipeline cases show. CoinJoin breaks clustering heuristics, Monero hides sender, receiver and amount by default, Zcash uses zk-SNARKs. Each has limits, and the law keeps moving.
